articles.title: Rising fuel prices 'cost Jersey tow truck business an extra £10k'
articles.summary: A business says fuel duty will need to be cut by 30p to 50p per litre to help.
articles.body:
Rising fuel prices are hitting businesses, with the owner of a vehicle breakdown service saying prices had cost his business between £9,000 and £11,000.

Oliver du Feu said it had a "big impact" because trucks, which held between 80 and 120 litres of diesel, were filled up every two days.

It comes as a proposition to lower fuel duty - currently about 65p per litre - by 10p per litre between October and December was withdrawn .

Jersey's treasury minister said there would be "targeted measures" in the government's budget to help people with the cost of living.

Fuel prices have continued to rise since the outbreak of the United States' war with Iran in February.

Du Feu said fuel duty would need to be reduced by 30p to 50p per litre to help businesses manage costs.

He said he expected prices to keep rising and, while his business had absorbed higher costs so far, he might have to charge customers more.

Treasury Minister Alan Maclean said duty cuts were a "blunt tool" and largely helped wealthier people.

Carl Walker, from the Jersey Consumer Council, said there was a "misconception" that fuel prices only impacted people who drove.

"Of everything that we consume in this island, 97% is imported.

"It needs fuel to get here and it needs fuel to be delivered... ultimately it will hit consumers in their pockets, even if they're literally buying a litre of milk in the shop."

The Jersey Consumer Council said the number of people using its fuel and food price comparison website had more than doubled since last year.

In the UK, the cost of petrol and diesel is the highest it has been since 2022 .

The government is set to publish a proposed budget by the end of September before it is debated in December.

Deputy Lucy Stephenson said she withdrew her proposition to cut fuel duty following "constructive discussions" with Maclean.

Maclean said he could not discuss budget measures as they were being developed.

He said it was "possible" people might feel worried that there would be no relief before next year.

He said: "Of course things are much more expensive than they were three years ago, but we've seen the pace of increases reduce slightly, which is encouraging.

"The first quarter of next year is going to be where people are likely to feel the greatest pressure, and that's what we're focusing on."

The director of ATF Fuels in Jersey, Jon Best, said: "Wholesale fuel prices have reached their highest level in four months.

"While the Channel Islands are geographically distant from the Middle East, they are not insulated from the global energy market.

"Fuel is traded in an international marketplace, meaning disruptions to supply, production, or distribution anywhere in the world can have a direct effect on local wholesale costs."

articles.title: Amazon Biggleswade warehouse plan prompt traffic concerns
articles.summary: A councillor is worried about the impact it may have on the A1 if traffic lights are installed.
articles.body:
Plans for an Amazon fulfilment centre that could create about 2,000 jobs would have a huge impact on a town's road network, a councillor said.

Amazon submitted a planning application to Central Bedfordshire Council for the robotics-enabled facility at Symmetry Park on Stratton Business Park, Biggleswade, earlier this year.

The facility would be positioned next to the A1 and have an internal footprint of about 1.4 million sq ft (130,064 sq m).

Grant Fage, a Conservative councillor for Biggleswade East, which includes the business park, said: "This is a very complicated application and will have huge impacts on Biggleswade, positively in terms of job creation but negatively for our road network."

Central Bedfordshire Council has set 18 November as a target date for a decision on the project.

Fage said on social media that Amazon's proposal for the Biggleswade Amazon Robotics Sortable (ARS) included making changes to the A1 south roundabout, such as installing traffic lights on approaches from the north and south.

"If [National Highways] confirm that signalisation is required, I hope it highlights the desperate state of the A1 in Biggleswade, given that we would have the only traffic lights on the entire A1 stretch between South Mimms and Scotland."

Fage said this would feel like a step backwards as it would lead to queuing traffic as the movement of vehicles would not be free flowing.

He added "this didn't work for the Black Cat Roundabout", which is currently undergoing a £1bn transformation .

The BBC has contacted National Highways for comment.

Amazon said it chose Biggleswade because it offered access to a "highly skilled labour market, which is essential for operating and maintaining the advanced robotics and automation systems within an ARS facility".

The warehouse would be accompanied by three additional units with an estimated construction spend of £300m, said the Local Democracy Reporting Service .

Tritax Big Box Developments, which owns Symmetry Park, said the backing of Amazon was a "strong endorsement of this location and reflects the scale of investment being made here".

In June, Amazon announced the official opening of its Northampton Robotics Sortable fulfilment centre, which can store tens of millions of products.

Mike Jackson, a spokesperson for Amazon, said: "Should the project progress, we would expect it to create a significant number of new roles in the area, with competitive pay and benefits."

Amazon is no stranger to Bedfordshire, where it already operates facilities in Dunstable and Houghton Regis.

articles.title: In 1988, Ohio attorney Neil McKown secretly bought 155 neglected acres; 38 years later, the family farms nearly 500 acres and he declined a $400,000-$500,000 timber cut to keep the woods
articles.summary: US News: What began as a secret land purchase has grown into a nearly 500-acre family farm built around conservation, forestry and a long-term commitment to th.
articles.body: What began as a secret land purchase has grown into a nearly 500-acre family farm built around conservation, forestry and a long-term commitment to the land. In 1988, Ohio attorney Neil McKown quietly purchased 155 acres without first telling his wife, Pamela. The property was overgrown, rundown and neglected, but what initially looked like a risky decision eventually became the foundation of a nearly 500-acre family farming operation. In a report based on interviews with the McKown family, Farm Progress detailed how the family transformed the land while maintaining its woods, improving drainage and adopting conservation practices. Their efforts have now earned the family the Ohio Conservation Farm Family Award. Most notably, McKown turned down an estimated $400,000 to $500,000 timber harvest because he preferred to keep the forest standing.A secret purchase that changed the family’s futureMcKown’s first step into farming was far from conventional. After practising law with his father, he wanted an escape from the pressures of legal work and the constant demands of computers, phones and clients. He had grown up in a small farming community about five miles from the property and had worked summer jobs on farms and at an agricultural fertiliser plant. The desire to spend more time outdoors eventually led him to the 155-acre property in 1988. McKown signed the purchase agreement without telling Pamela. He waited until he returned home before revealing what he had done. After dinner, he told his family to get into the car so they could see what they had bought.The first impression was not particularly promising. Pamela described the house and property as an eyesore, while much of the land was overgrown and neglected. Still, the family decided to take on the challenge.From neglected acreage to working farmThe McKowns began with only about 80 tillable acres, leaving the remainder as woods and pasture. Neil's first attempt at growing soybeans in 1990 even prompted three neighbouring farmers to stop by and examine his grain drill, apparently concerned about his lack of farming experience. Nevertheless, the family continued. They worked on the woods during winter, removing grapevines and undertaking timber-stand improvements with assistance from conservation cost-sharing programmes. The children, Sam and Lauren, were involved in the work while they were still young.The farm also presented a significant drainage challenge. Located in a prehistoric lake basin with sandy and silty soils, the property had only one inadequate drainage outlet and a few old drainage tiles. Working with a neighbouring farmer, the McKowns developed a drainage solution that connected their property to an existing system. They subsequently tiled the farmland systematically over five years and installed 30-foot buffer strips along the ditch.The operation steadily expandedThe original 155 acres eventually became part of a much larger operation. The family added cattle and hay equipment in the mid-1990s, while their son Sam became increasingly involved in the agricultural work. By the time he was 14, Sam had started doing custom hay work for local farmers. He continued the work through high school and college before eventually making farming his full-time livelihood.The family's biggest expansion came when they purchased a neighbouring 220-acre farm. The operation now covers nearly 500 acres, with crops and livestock forming part of the diversified agricultural system. The farm produces corn, soybeans, wheat, hay and alfalfa, while cattle are also raised. Highly erodible areas have been converted to pasture and managed through rotational grazing.Conservation is built into the farming systemAs the farm grew, the McKowns continued incorporating conservation practices rather than treating land protection as separate from agricultural production. They use vertical tillage in autumn followed by no-till planting in spring. The family also works with an agronomist and carries out grid soil sampling every three years to guide fertiliser applications. Their forestry management is particularly important to the family. They work with a professional forester and use selective harvesting to improve the condition of the woodland rather than treating the trees simply as a source of income. That philosophy became clear when the forester estimated that a more extensive timber cut could generate between $400,000 and $500,000. McKown declined, saying he would rather see the woods than cash in on the timber. The family has also removed invasive burning bush from the woodland and maintains an apiary and pond on the property.The farm has become an outdoor classroomThe McKowns have also used the property to introduce children to farming and natural ecosystems. Students from St. Mary’s and fifth-graders from Auburn and Shelby have visited for farm days. The family uses the property to teach about its agricultural history, glaciers and vernal pools. A naturalist from Gorman Nature Center has helped students understand the importance of the property's vernal pool, including its role in supporting salamanders and frogs.For the McKowns, the land has consequently become more than a place for producing crops and livestock. It has also become a setting where younger generations can learn about agriculture, conservation and the natural history of the region.A family operation moving into its next generationToday, Sam is a central part of the operation, managing much of the hay production. About 90% of the hay is sold to horse owners and cattle operations, while he also raises around 15 head of beef cattle. He has expanded his own agricultural holdings by purchasing 130 acres near Ontario, Ohio, where he grows alfalfa and row crops. Forty acres there are enrolled in a 15-year Conservation Reserve Program reforestation programme. His sister Lauren pursued a different career and works for OhioHealth in Columbus, but the family's connection to the farm remains central to the story of its development.A long-term view of the landThe McKowns' transformation of the property has taken nearly four decades. What started with an unexpected 155-acre purchase has developed into a nearly 500-acre farming operation recognised for its conservation practices. For Neil, the land represents something that extends beyond its immediate economic value. His decision to preserve the woods despite the potential for a $400,000-$500,000 timber harvest reflects the family's broader approach: improving the land while maintaining the natural features that make it valuable.The Ohio Conservation Farm Family Award recognises the family's conservation efforts alongside its agricultural work. And after 38 years, what McKown once described as his "pipe dream" has become a family enterprise in which farming, conservation, forestry and education continue side by side.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Indonesia replanted mangroves on Flores in 2013; 10 years later, restored forests supported 10 fauna species and stored up to 70 Mg CO2 per hectare
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Indonesia’s Flores Island was the site of a mangrove reforestation project launched in 2013, with native seedlings planted along the coast between End.
articles.body: Indonesia’s Flores Island was the site of a mangrove reforestation project launched in 2013, with native seedlings planted along the coast between Ende and Sikka. Ten years later, researchers surveyed restored areas at Bangkoor, Kolisia and Talibura to assess plant and animal diversity, carbon sequestration and energy storage. The study recorded 10 mangrove species and 10 fauna species across the three sites. Kolisia had the highest mangrove species richness, while Talibura had the highest fauna species richness. Restored stands also recorded carbon sequestration, although the researchers found differences in vegetation development between the three locations after a decade.What did scientists find in Indonesia’s replanted Flores mangrovesAccording to the study published in Scientific Reports titled ‘Mangroves, fauna compositions and carbon sequestration after ten years restoration on Flores Island, Indonesia’, the survey identified 10 mangrove species from six families across the three locations. Kolisia recorded the highest plant species richness, with eight species, followed by Bangkoor with seven and Talibura with five. The study found that Kolisia had the highest vegetation diversity, while Talibura had a large number of seedlings and saplings.The researchers also identified 10 fauna species across the three reforestation sites. Talibura recorded the highest fauna species richness, with eight species, followed by Bangkoor with seven and Kolisia with six. The animals included the crab-eating macaque (Macaca fascicularis), which the study lists as endangered, along with mudskippers, bivalves, crabs, gastropods, reptiles and birds.Mangrove restoration stored up to 70.02 Mg CO2 per hectareAfter 10 years of reforestation, carbon sequestration in the restored mangrove stands ranged from 28.69 to 70.02 Mg CO2 per hectare. Energy storage ranged from 30.54 × 10⁴ to 54.07 × 10⁴ MJ per hectare. These figures were calculated for Bangkoor and Kolisia because no poles or trees were recorded at Talibura during the assessment.At species level, Rhizophora apiculata had the highest carbon sequestration value, at 47.37 ± 5.68 kg CO2. Bruguiera gymnorhiza recorded the highest energy storage value, at 645.22 ± 201.65 MJ. The researchers estimated carbon and energy storage using above-ground biomass rather than destructive sampling. Carbon storage was calculated using a factor of 0.47.Mangrove species varied across Flores restoration sitesThe researchers found similarities in plant and animal communities between the three restoration sites, although some species occurred only at particular locations. Avicennia marina was recorded only at Kolisia, while Excoecaria agallocha and Lumnitzera rasemosa were recorded only at Bangkoor. Among the animals, Varanus salvator was recorded at Kolisia, while Macaca fascicularis was recorded at Bangkoor.The study found differences in the development of the restored mangroves after 10 years. The researchers reported relatively low levels of species richness, heterogeneity and evenness across the mangrove ecosystems. Talibura had the greatest water depth of the three sites, fewer mangrove species and no poles or trees recorded during the survey. The researchers recommended continued long-term monitoring of mangrove health, resilience and ecological changes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: No criminal charges in death of Nolan Wells, grand jury finds
articles.summary: A grand jury will not pursue criminal charges in the death of Nolan Wells, the local district attorney said, forcefully rejecting months of speculation that race played a role in the death of the Mississippi teen this summer.
articles.body: A grand jury will not pursue charges in the death of Nolan Wells, the local district attorney said Monday, forcefully rejecting months of speculation that race played a role in the death of the Mississippi teenager this summer. District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath made the announcement in a video message, saying the grand jury returned a “no true bill,” meaning it did not find sufficient evidence to indict anyone with a crime. A partially redacted copy of the grand jury report was also posted to the DA’s Facebook page. Wells, 18, was with friends celebrating July Fourth and was last seen on Horn Island, a barrier reef off Mississippi accessible only by boat. His body was found at the northwestern tip of the island July 6, his family’s lawyer said. “There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan’s disappearance and death were racially motivated,” Myers McIlrath said. “Nolan’s friends loved Nolan, and Nolan loved them. Nolan chose to stay on the island that day, and there is not a scintilla of evidence to contradict that.” The family’s lawyer, civil rights attorney Ben Crump, previously called into question whether race was a factor in Wells’ death, as it appeared Wells was one of a few Black people there that day. On Monday, Myers McIlrath took direct aim at Crump and his team, saying they also previously informed her office that they’d found no evidence a crime had been committed against Wells. “I’m not suggesting that a grieving mother police the rumors surrounding her child’s death,” the DA said. “What I am suggesting is that the Crump team knew better but did not do better.” Crump in turn said a statement Tuesday, “This grand jury result leaves us with more questions than answers. Nolan’s family will not rest until we know what happened to him, and neither will we.” “Mississippi’s own pathologist found two bruises on the back of this young man’s head ... An independent autopsy documented traces of blood and recent blunt force injuries to the back of Nolan’s head and his back. To this day, not one person has explained how they got there,” he added. “We don’t know how Nolan died, and neither does the State of Mississippi. Mississippi must keep investigating,” Crump said. Wells’ parents are expected to make a public address later Tuesday. The grand jury issued 132 subpoenas and heard from 43 witnesses, and seven people were invited to testify before the panel, according to the partially redacted report. It was made up of 23 grand jurors from a “cross section of citizens” from Jackson County between 27 and 68 of age, it said. Among them were 13 men and 10 women, including “12 Caucasians, five African Americans, one Asian, two Hispanics, two Native Americans and one individual who preferred ‘other,’” it said. “The grand jury finds no credible evidence to support the public allegations that any persons who rode to or from Horn Island on July 4, 2026 ... engaged in any criminal conduct related to ​the death of Mr. Wells,” the report released by McIlrath’s office said. Wells was last seen sometime in the afternoon of July 4. Friends told police that they had to leave early because their boat started taking on water but that Wells chose to stay and catch a ride back later with others. The grand jury report found that it was common for people on Horn Island to “socialize on boats and in the water,” and that it was “not unusual or suspicious” for people to return from the island on different boats. It concluded there was no evidence that Wells had any sort of physical altercation or argument with anyone the day he was last seen. It added “that the position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr. Wells’ body is consistent with drowning.” Crump and Wells’ family have previously rejected notions that he drowned, saying he was athletic and a good swimmer. An independent autopsy commissioned by the family’s legal team found that the teenager’s cause and manner of death were “undetermined.” The state’s chief medical examiner and a forensic pathologist retained by Wells’ family both “opined that the cause and manner of Mr. Wells’ death is undetermined and that drowning is a diagnosis of exclusion,” according to the grand jury report. It noted, however, that neither has ruled out accidental drowning as a cause. Wells’ funeral July 20 attracted hundreds of people. “Your absence has left an emptiness that can never truly be filled,” his mother, Christine Wells-Wonsley, said at the time. “In a world that can often feel dark, be like Nolan, be the light that brightens the lives of those around you.”

articles.title: Palestinians turn to communal ovens to bake bread in Gaza
articles.summary: Amid Gaza’s food crisis, bread remains a staple as displaced families use communal ovens to save on costly fuel.
articles.body:
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Every morning, Azza Ashour kneads dough for her five children before carrying it to a communal oven at the school where her family has been sheltering.

The 31-year-old mother has little money, no regular income and no husband at home. She explained that he has been detained by the Israeli army since May 2024, one of thousands of Palestinians locked away without trial by Israel.

Azza makes the dough stretch as far as possible, sometimes filling the bread with cheese or a little chocolate. If there is little else to feed the children, the bread itself becomes the meal.

“One piece of dough can keep my children going for breakfast, lunch and dinner,” she said.

Azza is from Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza, an area destroyed by Israel during its genocidal war. The family was first displaced to southern Gaza, before eventually settling at Cairo School in western Gaza City. It has been turned into a displacement centre where they have lived for around a year.

She is now responsible for managing the household and caring for all five children.

“I have been managing a family on my own for three years,” she said. “It’s a huge responsibility.”

Her family receives canned food assistance from the World Food Programme, but sometimes only once a month or every two months.

With little money for food and no income of her own, bread has become central to how she feeds her children.

The cost of cooking is another obstacle. Azza says she cannot afford to regularly buy firewood or fuel, which has become too expensive for her family.

That’s where the communal oven comes in. Supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), it allows the displaced to bake their dough for free.

Before the oven, Azza says buying bread could cost her about 15 shekels ($5) a day.

“Honestly, this oven is the most important thing,” she said. “Bread is so valuable to us.”

From feeding children to earning for them

A few steps from where Azza collects her bread, Randa Adwan is working as a baker.

The 38-year-old mother of seven wakes up at about 5:30am to prepare dough for her children before they leave for school. By 7am, she begins her shift at the oven, baking for families until noon.

She pauses, wiping her face with a towel. The heat and the hours of work are taking their toll.

“It is tiring. It really is tiring,” she said. “I go home and sleep. My hands hurt, my back hurts, I have headaches. It is exhausting.”

Randa has a bachelor’s degree in education. She never imagined that she would one day find herself working at a communal oven, baking bread for displaced families.

But the circumstances of the war left her with little choice, she said.

Working at the bakery is a privilege. With few jobs available in Gaza and Palestinians desperate for any kind of income, bakers are selected through a lottery for a one month work placement.

This is Randa’s second time being chosen and she earns 70 shekels ($23) a day.

“It is good for us because there is no money,” she said. “Firewood is expensive, the situation is difficult and thank God I was selected. At least I have something to spend on my children.”

Before the war, Randa’s husband ran a shop and supported her and their seven children. Now he is unemployed and Randa has had to take on the responsibility.

“Now I have to provide everything for me and my children… food, clothes, water, everything,” she said.

The oven at Cairo School is part of an ICRC programme supporting communal ovens in schools and shelters across Gaza.

At the shelter, 220 households live permanently and six ovens operate there. Nearby communities can also access the service.

The ICRC pays for the ovens and the wages of the workers who operate them. Families prepare their dough and bring it to be baked between 7am and noon.

Each oven can produce up to 200 loaves a day, according to the ICRC.

Across Gaza, the organisation supports 179 communal ovens. From January to June, they produced 9.2 million loaves for about 44,000 people.

“For people that have no place to stay, they have no purchasing power to buy necessities in the market,” said Matthew Manguet, the ICRC’s Livelihoods Manager.

“Even the goods that are available in the market are quite costly, so they cannot afford them.”

The project emerged during the war for displaced people in need.

“During the conflict, there was a lack of access to bread and people, due to displacement, didn’t have the space to cook their own food,” Manguet said. “They don’t have access to cooking fuel, firewood.”

The ovens also provide a small source of paid work for women such as Randa, at a time when traditional sources of income have been disrupted.

Manguet said more than 80 percent of people in Gaza have no job, while access to agriculture and fishing – important sources of livelihoods before the crisis – remains limited as a result of Israeli restrictions and damage inflicted during the war.

The demand for the ovens is also changing as displacement continues. Manguet said the ICRC has been increasing the number of ovens across Gaza as more families arrive at shelters.

“We’re even increasing the number of ovens across the Strip based on the number of people that continue to be displaced,” he said. “So we don’t see a decrease, at least in the near future.”

For the ICRC, the ovens are only one response to needs that remain much larger than the programme itself.

“It’s a small drop in the ocean,” Manguet said. “But it makes a difference.”

For families living in small tents with little space to cook, access to an oven can determine whether the food they have can become a meal.

Back at the school, that difference is measured in dough, bread and the hours women spend making both possible.

Randa returns to her tent after each shift to her seven children, trying to meet their needs with what little she earns.

She says families here are all living through the same struggle, trying to get through each day and secure even the most basic food and water.

“Any initiative that helps improve our lives means a lot to us. Life is very difficult and displacement is painful. There are so many things we need just to live.”

articles.title: Undermining the UN is not a new US policy
articles.summary: While acting as the official host for the UN, the US has sought to weaken it for decades.
articles.body:
The annual general debate of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) starts on Tuesday morning in New York amid dire circumstances. Besides traffic gridlock and overpriced hotel rates, cavalcades of motorcades and successive dignitaries delivering calibrated speeches, this session will hear Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’s last speech on the state of the UN.

Guterres headed the UN for 10 years, and during that time, he repeatedly failed to defend it when it came under attack. He passes on his post at the top of a world organisation on the verge of financial collapse and more marginalised than ever before.

Paradoxically, Guterres has the United States, the host government of the UN, and its mercurial president, Donald Trump, to thank for this dismal state of affairs.

Earlier this year, the Trump administration withdrew from dozens of UN agencies and organs and, in an extraordinary move, ceased all payments of its dues to the regular and peacekeeping budgets of the UN. But these drastic policy decisions did not spring out of nowhere. Trump’s unhappiness with the UN is multifaceted, and his decision to stop fulfilling Washington’s legally binding financial obligation may well be the logical culmination of decades-long US policy.

In the mid-1980s, the Reagan administration accused the UN of being a third-world, anti-US forum. To compel the organisation to better serve its interests and under the guise of the ubiquitous need for reform, which all secretaries-general fell for, the US started to withhold a share of its assessed contribution, which accounted for a quarter of the regular budget and a third of the peacekeeping budget back then.

By 1987, the US relaxed its payment withholding policy, but the precedent was set. Washington continued to use the threat of withholding payment to maintain its grip on an organisation it viewed and continues to view as a vehicle serving its national interests rather than a multilateral agent serving the whole of humanity.

Ever since the Reagan years, the US has kept the UN on a short financial leash, and to this day, has been deliberately accruing arrears. It currently owes an estimated $4.2bn – that is equivalent to 120 percent of the regular UN budget for 2026.

Trump has readily embraced this policy of financial blackmail. His administration has slow-walked mandatory payments, although earlier this month it paid $827m towards its outstanding dues so it could preserve its voting rights in the UNGA.

The president’s ambivalent view of the UN may be rooted in a lesser-known detail. In 2001, Trump, then a real estate developer, lobbied then Secretary-General Kofi Annan to be awarded the billion-dollar renovation project of the UN headquarters, but he did not get his way. That was probably not forgotten.

But just like during the Reagan years, there is another major factor driving Trump’s assault on the UN: US congressional politics. As Israel faced growing backlash at the UN for its genocide in Gaza, pressure from the Israeli lobby in Washington mounted. The Iron Dome diplomatic cover the US provided to Israel in the UN Security Council (UNSC) was no longer sufficient.

By 2025, two years into the genocidal campaign, Guterres’s tepid and overdue criticisms of Israeli policies, critical UNGA resolutions and scathing reports by special rapporteurs of the Human Rights Council – including Francesca Albanese, whom Washington placed under sanctions in violation of its host country obligations – became too much for Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the US Congress.

In the 1980s, Washington deemed the UN a third-world anti-US forum; today, it is deemed anti-Israel and anti-Semitic. The US’s blind and unconditional support for Israel has brought it growing isolation at the UN, as has its decision to launch a war of aggression against Iran.

Against the backdrop of these developments, the selection of the next secretary-general is dominating the behind-the-scenes agenda. Guterres’s lacklustre tenure at the helm of an organisation on the verge of financial bankruptcy and political demise will soon be forgotten. But what should be remembered is that his appeasement policy vis-a-vis Washington since the first Trump administration has evidently failed.

The new secretary-general will inherit the modus vivendi under which all secretaries-general since Javier Perez de Cuellar have had to operate — chronic cash flow problems due to US arrears.

That should motivate the new UN leadership to consider an overhaul of how the UN budget is put together and how member states’ contributions are allocated. Leaving the power of the purse in Washington’s hands is a self-inflicted perpetual wound that could prove lethal for the organisation.

Another fundamental question is whether the UN would be better off had its headquarters not been in the US. For too long, Washington has seen the UN either as a vector of its national interests or in adversarial terms. It has even used its position as a host to exclude world leaders it has viewed as hostile or undesirable, such as PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat and today Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas.

Evidently, those are decisions only the UNGA can take. But a secretary-general with foresight and political backbone ought to provide views and leadership on those seminal questions to save the organisation from further marginalisation and possible demise.

articles.title: In 2011, researchers scanning satellite images over Libya spotted faint desert shapes; field surveys helped reveal more than 100 Garamantian farms, villages and forts in the Sahara
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Satellite imagery reveals over 100 Roman-era farms, villages, and forts in Libya's Sahara, changing our understanding of ancient Saharan civilization and trade routes.
articles.body: For many years, outsiders saw the deep heart of Libya's southwestern desert as barren, hostile territory with little to offer archaeologists other than sporadic Roman allusions to unruly desert tribes. Since international researchers had little access to the area and the region's pre-Islamic history was rarely a state priority, this impression remained largely unquestioned for decades. Uncovering what had been concealed beneath the sand for two millennia would take modern satellite technology paired with whatever narrow access to the ground researchers could manage.A study team from the University of Leicester led by Professor David Mattingly spent years sifting through high-quality satellite data of the Fezzan area, some of it collected originally for oil sector assessments, as well as aerial photographs shot decades earlier in the 1950s and 1960s, before finally securing a narrow window to test their findings on the ground in early 2011. The imagery that emerged from this research was shocking to the team. Scattered across the desert were faint geometric forms that turned out to be the remains of fortified farms, walled villages and many fortified towns, constructions that, unlike the partially excavated Garamantian capital nearby, had never been systematically surveyed or recorded.Faces behind the fortressesThe villages were built by the Garamantes, an indigenous Saharan people known previously only through hostile Roman and Greek texts that depicted them as rebellious nomads on the edge of empire. The satellite evidence suggested a rather different story. They discovered the mud brick remains of castle-like compounds, walls still four metres high, and cairn cemeteries, wells and faint traces of field systems and irrigation networks that once supported oasis farming in a landscape that now receives virtually no rainfall. The study itself, known as Trans Sahara, was supported by a European Research Council Advanced Grant. The funding body’s own description of the discovery calls it one of the most important archaeological finds to emerge from remote sensing work in North Africa.Over a hundred fortified farms, towns and forts were listed in all, most of which date to between the first and fifth centuries AD, a time that saw the Garamantes very much as near neighbours to the Roman Empire rather than outside its awareness entirely. The findings showed an organised state with towns, a written language and technologies capable of supporting agriculture in some of the most inhospitable terrain on Earth, as well as an active role in opening up trade routes across the Sahara that linked the Mediterranean world with regions further south.Confirming the finding on the groundSatellite pictures could indicate that the structures are ancient, but a real expedition would be the only way to validate them. The chronology revealed by the aerial evidence was corroborated by samples of Garamantian pottery acquired during a field survey the researchers were able to do in early 2011, before the team had to leave the country due to the civil strife that finally led to the overthrow of Gaddafi's administration. As the political situation calmed in the years that followed, further ground surveys were undertaken, confirming the pre-Islamic antiquity of the ruins and the remarkable level of their preservation.The capital of the Garamantes, the ancient city of Garama, today the site of Jarma, had already been partially excavated. But the newly identified settlements in the vicinity were so extensive that they changed the view from a single important city to an entire network of interconnected communities. Later, the research information service of the European Commission itself, CORDIS, presented the findings for a broader audience, saying the revelation was overturning our knowledge of early African state development.There was also a symbolic significance to the discovery for Libyan heritage authorities beyond archaeology, as these were the first significant towns in the region not constructed by outside colonial forces such as the Greeks or Romans. The search of satellite pixels results in the restoration of a whole civilisation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2011, North Carolina hiker Jennifer Pharr Davis started the Appalachian Trail in Maine; 46 days later, she reached Georgia after hiking roughly 2,180 miles faster than anyone before
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 2011, Jennifer Pharr Davis completed the Appalachian Trail in 46 days, setting a record after hiking roughly 2,180 miles from Maine to Georgia.
articles.body: For over four decades, the Appalachian Trail’s record for quickest hiking was held solely by males, usually ultra runners who trekked thirty to fifty miles a day in closely controlled eleven to thirteen-hour periods. That pattern had held so strongly that when a person from outside the running community set out to disrupt it in the summer of 2011, few onlookers gave the attempt any credence. The result shattered decades of assumptions about who could dominate the toughest long-distance trail in the United States and how such a feat should be undertaken.But when she decided to pursue the overall record, Jennifer Pharr Davis, a hiker from Hendersonville, North Carolina, was already a seasoned Appalachian Trail veteran. In 2005, after graduating from university, she hiked the path for the first time and set the women’s speed record of 57 days in 2008. Davis’ approach was based solely on hiking rather than on the running-heavy strategy of past record holders. She trained by walking rather than running, believing that her long, steady, high-mileage walking speed, which she could maintain for sixteen hours a day, would outlast the shorter, faster bursts preferred by trail runners.A stroll strategy, not a run approachDavis began her quest on 16 June 2011 from Mount Katahdin in Maine, walking south towards Springer Mountain in Georgia, waking most days about 4:45 in the morning and hiking well into darkness. She had a support group, including her husband, Brew Davis, and veteran endurance hiker Warren Doyle, who assisted in handling logistics along the way while she concentrated on moving forward. The trail, which passes through fourteen states, six national parks and eight national forests over approximately 2,180 miles, was a punishing combination of steep climbs, root-strewn descents and unpredictable weather that made maintaining a consistent pace extraordinarily difficult, the National Park Service claimed.On her travels, Davis saw thirty-six bears, along with moose and porcupines, and witnessed every dawn and sunset of her trip. The pace increased rather than lessened as she approached the finish. She needed a sixty-mile day towards the very end of her effort, quickly followed by another day of more than thirty-six miles, to secure the record within her target window. The physical toll included blistered feet, persistent exhaustion and sleep deprivation so severe it would break most athletes well before the finish line was in sight.Beating a record set by men decades agoDavis arrived at Springer Mountain on July 31, 2011, finishing the path in 46 days, 11 hours and 20 minutes, beating the previous overall record by 26 hours and averaging almost 47 miles of trekking each day. She was not only the quickest woman, but she also became the first woman to ever hold the outright fastest known time on the Appalachian Trail, a title no woman had held in the entire history of organised speed efforts on the trail. Her achievement is listed on Fastest Known Time, an internet registry that collects and certifies such records on important long-distance trails throughout the world.Her achievement was not uniformly received. Later Davis remembered being met with disbelief from some who questioned if she had really completed the whole trip or could legitimately have maintained such a daily mileage. That scrutiny was a reflection of broader beliefs at the time about what women were capable of in ultra-endurance sport, assumptions her success helped destroy. She subsequently served three years on the board of directors of the Appalachian Trail Conservancy, the nonprofit organisation that partners with the National Park Service to maintain and protect the trail, a role that linked her first-hand hiking accomplishment to the institutional effort of preserving the footpath for future generations.Davis’ overall record would stand for four years until ultra runner Scott Jurek shattered it in 2015. Since then the outright title has returned to endurance racers. Still, her 2011 walk remains a watershed moment in the sport, credited with helping to usher in an era where women now regularly compete with and beat men across the world’s longest ultra distance trail records. For the feat, Davis was named National Geographic’s Adventurer of the Year in 2012 and went on to found her own guiding company and continue pushing physical boundaries in the years to come, including backpacking hundreds of miles while pregnant and hiking with her young children in all fifty states. Her Appalachian Trail walk is evidence that an innovative approach, built on discipline rather than raw speed, could outperform decades of established wisdom on one of the world's most demanding trails.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: No regular contact with couple held in Iran, family say
articles.summary: Craig and Lindsay Foreman's family say they were promised contact after they ended hunger strikes.
articles.body:
A British couple who have been detained in Iran for more than 20 months have not had regular contact restored with their family, despite assurances, their family say.

Lindsay and Craig Foreman, who were sentenced to 10 years in jail over espionage charges which they deny, were promised family contact after they ended hunger strikes , but there had not been regular calls since, they said.

The family of the couple, who are from East Sussex, is calling for an urgent meeting with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband to discuss what action can be taken.

The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) said the couple's welfare was its "top priority" and officials had been working to provide assistance.

It said this included the ambassador visiting the pair in prison and facilitating calls with their family back in the UK.

The couple began hunger strikes earlier this year, after claiming that prison authorities had began to prevent them from speaking to their families. The hunger strikes lasted 93 and 84 days respectively.

The family is now calling for the government to provide regular consular visits and implement a focused strategy to secure the couple's release.

A spokesperson for the family says a British consular visit is planned for 5 October, which they say will be just the second visit of 2026.

They said the length of time it took to arrange the meeting, particularly following the hunger strikes, was "extremely concerning".

The FCDO said the family met with Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty and the UK's envoy for complex consular detentions Alistair Burt in August.

A spokesperson for the office said Doughty "set out how unjustified and appalling we consider Lindsay and Craig's incarceration to be, and the action that the UK Government is taking to try and secure their release".

Joe Bennett, Lindsay's son, said: "I understand perfectly well that the British government cannot simply tell the Iranian authorities what to do. I have never expected that.

"What I do expect is for our government to stand up for its citizens, to challenge what is happening and to keep pushing when commitments are made and then not honoured.

"Mum and Craig brought their hunger strikes to an end believing things would improve. Regular calls were supposed to be part of that.

"Instead, we are once again in a position where we are waiting, trying to understand what is happening from a distance and being given another date further down the road. That cannot just become normal."

Bennett, who is from Folkestone, in Kent, says he wants a meeting with Miliband to understand what is being done to bring the couple back to Britain.

"After everything Mum and Craig have been through, it is reasonable for us to ask whether every possible avenue is genuinely being explored and whether this case is being treated with the urgency it deserves," he added.

Bennett said he wanted Miliband to hear the case "directly from the family".

"After more than 600 days, I do not think that is too much to ask," he added.

articles.title: In 2024, a Greek woman crossed Nepal's Great Himalaya Trail on foot in 52 days, setting the fastest female time on the route
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Greek endurance athlete Asimina Inglezou completed Nepal’s Great Himalaya Trail on foot in 52 days, 6 hours and 23 minutes in 2024, earning the Guinne.
articles.body: Greek endurance athlete Asimina Inglezou completed Nepal’s Great Himalaya Trail on foot in 52 days, 6 hours and 23 minutes in 2024, earning the Guinness World Records title for the fastest female completion of the route. She undertook the challenge as part of the 2024 Great Himal Race, a demanding west-to-east crossing of Nepal that began in Hilsa and finished in the Kanchenjunga region. The journey took her through remote Himalayan landscapes, steep mountain terrain and routes involving substantial elevation changes. The event required participants to maintain their progress over several weeks while navigating challenging conditions. Inglezou’s achievement placed her among the athletes who completed the demanding Himalayan crossing and made her the first woman to reach the finish during that edition of the race.Asimina Inglezou crossed Nepal's Great Himalaya Trail on foot in 52 daysGuinness World Records officially recognises Asimina Inglezou for the fastest completion of the Great Himalaya Trail on foot by a female. Her recorded time was 52 days, 6 hours and 23 minutes, with the achievement taking place in Nepal between 9 April and 31 May 2024. Inglezou completed the journey during the Great Himal Race, which brought together endurance athletes attempting to cross the country’s Himalayan region. The Guinness record identifies the specific category as a female achievement completed on foot. This distinction is important because the Great Himalaya Trail consists of a network of routes rather than one single, uniformly marked path. Inglezou’s record therefore relates to the official category and the conditions under which the crossing was completed.The race began in western NepalThe 2024 Great Himal Race started in Hilsa, in western Nepal, and continued towards the Kanchenjunga region in the east. The event organiser, Les Chevaliers du Vent, described the route as covering approximately 1,602 kilometres, with around 90,310 metres of positive elevation gain and 88,817 metres of descent. The journey was designed as a west-to-east crossing through the Nepalese Himalayas, bringing participants across varied mountain environments. Competitors were given flexibility in choosing their routes, meaning that their individual journeys could differ in distance, elevation and the trails they followed. The route passed through remote regions and included sections where traditional mountain paths had been affected by road construction and changing local infrastructure.Participants navigated challenging Himalayan terrainUnlike a conventional race that follows one fixed course, the Great Himal Race allowed participants to select routes through the Himalayan landscape. The organiser reported that competitors travelled through regions including Upper Dolpo, Dhorpatan, Upper Mustang and the Everest area, depending on their chosen paths. Some participants also crossed mountain passes above 5,000 metres, adding to the physical demands of the crossing. The combination of long distances, steep climbs and high-altitude terrain required competitors to manage their pace and make route decisions throughout the journey. The changing condition of the trails also created practical challenges. Participants had to adapt to the landscape while continuing towards the finish in the Kanchenjunga region. These conditions made navigation and sustained endurance important elements of the event.Inglezou became the first female finisherInglezou was one of three women who began the 2024 Great Himal Race. She became the first female participant to reach the finish at the Kanchenjunga Base Camp region. Canadian runner Rachelle Komarnisky was also reported to have completed the full crossing on foot. The event organiser listed Inglezou’s racing time as 367 hours and 35 minutes, while Komarnisky recorded 393 hours and 46 minutes. These figures formed part of the event’s results, while Guinness World Records recorded Inglezou’s overall completion time as 52 days, 6 hours and 23 minutes. The difference reflects the way racing time and total elapsed time were reported. Inglezou’s achievement was subsequently recognised under the Guinness category for the fastest female completion of the Great Himalaya Trail on foot.The crossing involved significant elevation gainThe scale of the journey was measured not only by its distance but also by the amount of climbing and descending involved. According to the event organiser, participants faced more than 90,000 metres of positive elevation gain across the route. Repeated ascents and descents placed sustained demands on competitors, particularly when combined with high-altitude conditions and remote trails. The route’s flexibility meant that individual participants could experience different mountain passes and landscapes. Some sections required travel through areas where access to facilities and established infrastructure was limited. Competitors therefore had to manage their energy and progress over an extended period. Inglezou’s successful completion demonstrated the endurance required to maintain a long-distance journey across Nepal’s mountainous terrain.The 2024 event attracted international competitorsThe Great Himal Race brought together participants from different countries and backgrounds in endurance sports. The organiser reported that 26 people initially intended to undertake the full crossing, while 22 eventually reached the Kanchenjunga Base Camp area. Thirteen participants were reported to have completed the high-Himalaya crossing on foot. The race included competitors who travelled through different routes and faced varying terrain along the way. Because participants had flexibility in route selection, the event did not involve identical experiences for every runner. The results reflected the challenges of completing the crossing, with competitors required to sustain their efforts over several weeks. Inglezou’s performance stood out within the female category, as she reached the finish first among the women taking part in that edition.What made the achievement notableCompleting the Great Himalaya Trail requires prolonged physical effort, route planning and the ability to adapt to changing mountain conditions. The 2024 race combined long-distance travel with substantial elevation gain and high-altitude sections. Participants had to maintain progress while dealing with steep terrain and the practical challenges of crossing remote parts of Nepal. Inglezou completed the journey in more than 52 days, making the achievement an example of sustained endurance rather than a short-distance speed performance. Her record also came within a specific female category, which Guinness World Records officially recognised. The achievement highlights the difficulty of undertaking a long Himalayan crossing on foot, particularly when the route includes substantial climbs, descents and varying trail conditions.Guinness World Records confirms the female recordGuinness World Records lists Asimina Inglezou of Greece as the holder of the record for the fastest completion of the Great Himalaya Trail on foot by a female. Her official time was 52 days, 6 hours and 23 minutes, and the achievement took place in Nepal between 9 April and 31 May 2024. She completed the journey as part of the Great Himal Race, which crossed Nepal from Hilsa in the west towards the Kanchenjunga region in the east. The event’s route involved approximately 1,602 kilometres and significant elevation gain, according to its organiser. By reaching the finish during the 2024 race, Inglezou became the first female finisher and secured a Guinness World Records title for her performance across the Nepalese Himalayas.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Russia forced a captured Ukrainian soldier to make a propaganda video. His village refused to bury him.
articles.summary: Russia has coerced thousands of Ukrainian prisoners to denounce their leaders and country in propaganda videos. The consequences can follow them home.
articles.body: KARPYLIVKA, Ukraine — Volodymyr Srebrodolskyy, a Ukrainian soldier with gray hair and deep wrinkles, smoked a cigarette while speaking to his Russian captor behind the camera. “I don’t want to go back there,” Srebrodolskyy said, appearing to have turned against his country. “It would be good if all of this ended quickly.” The video was Russian propaganda. Weeks before it was posted on Telegram, Srebrodolskyy was fighting for Ukraine on the eastern front line against the men who captured him. Now, he was following their script. The propaganda worked. Arguments over whether Srebrodolskyy betrayed his country tore apart his hometown of Karpylivka, a village of 500 nestled in the golden wheat fields of Ukraine’s Chernihiv region. Some labeled him a traitor. “He’s smoking a cigarette, saying he won’t return to Ukraine,” said Nina Bedko, 68, who stopped to chat with other women along Karpylivka’s main street. “That’s why people got that impression.” Srebrodolskyy died in captivity weeks after the video was shared. When his body was ready for burial this spring, some of his neighbors — believing the propaganda — threatened violence against the village mayor if he allowed Srebrodolskyy to be placed in the town’s cemetery. Others defended him, saying he went to war willingly, without trying to evade the draft. “Maybe they promised him mountains of gold,” said his cousin, Lidia Kovalenko, a short 82-year-old woman with a bright smile. “At least they could have buried him near his mother.” The arguments put the fate of his body in limbo. Thousands of such videos have been posted to Russian social media channels, some of them airing on state-run television. They follow a formula: Ukrainian prisoners decry their commanders, decline to return home, denounce corruption and say they hope for the war to end soon. The message has been repeated since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 with few variations, reinforcing Russian narratives about the country it invaded and seeding distrust toward the army in Ukrainian communities. A system of abuse Human rights organizations have called on Russia to stop broadcasting videos of prisoners of war since the early days of the full-scale invasion. “The obligation under the Geneva Conventions is to protect POWs from being objects of public curiosity, as well as from intimidation or humiliation,” Aisling Reidy, senior legal adviser at Human Rights Watch, said in a statement at the time. The videos are recorded inside a detention system the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission to Ukraine has found to be systematically abusive — sustained in part by “dehumanizing language in state-owned media.” In interviews with more than 850 Ukrainian prisoners of war conducted by the U.N., 96% said they endured torture or mistreatment, including beatings, electric shocks to the genitals, sleep deprivation and mock executions. The abuse can last for years, the report says. Over half of Russian prisoners of war have also reported mistreatment to U.N. investigators, saying it took place at the point of capture. Russian prisoners have been made to film similar videos, which the U.N. has condemned. However, unlike Russia, Ukraine allows monitoring groups unhindered access to the facilities holding the prisoners, which the U.N. says are compliant with the Geneva Conventions. The Media Initiative for Human Rights, a Ukrainian nonprofit, has documented 240 detention facilities holding Ukrainians on occupied and Russian territory. “The more of these videos they record, the more they will give power to their ideas,” said Olena Belyachkova, whose work at MIHR focuses on the imprisoned and the missing. Her own husband endured Russian captivity from 2015 to 2017. In some cases, Russia has used propaganda videos as evidence to prosecute Ukrainian prisoners. Belyachkova said that in the absence of an official Russian accounting, the videos can serve as proof of a soldier’s status as a prisoner of war. Because they are frequently deleted from social media, the exact number of such videos cannot be quantified, but they number in the thousands, she said. The industry When Vasylyna Duman saw a video online of her husband, Yevhen Shybalov, from Russian captivity, her first reaction was to keep it secret. She worried that a media storm would raise the price Russia would ask to exchange him. This was the first time she saw his face in months. Shybalov volunteered to fight on the first day of the invasion. Russians captured him in May 2022. In the video, he was thin and bore signs of beatings, she said. She filed a police report using the video as evidence of his captivity. She wanted it on record that he was forced to speak against his will. “To get a video is a big happiness, even if the person says something weird on it,” she said. It meant he was alive. Shybalov, a tall man with pronounced cheekbones, watched the Russian occupation unfold in Donetsk city as Russian operatives and their collaborators poured into Ukraine’s east in 2014. The Ukrainian government was in disarray after the Revolution of Dignity overthrew a pro-Russian president, limiting its ability to respond. “It gave Russian propaganda a free space without competitors,” he said of the chaos of that time. “It made people very disoriented about what’s happening.” Previously a journalist, Shybalov quit to launch an aid organization with an office in a Donetsk hotel that provided them free space. One day, he saw a Russian television crew of about 50 move into the same hotel. Shybalov watched them learn lines for the roles of local residents. “They just drank coffee, smoked cigarettes on the veranda and learned to say, ‘I’m from Horlivka,’” Shybalov said. Then they would wonder, “What the f—k is Horlivka?” Some of the civilians Shybalov delivered aid to believed the Russian propaganda. He did not argue with them. “They were just victims,” he said. “They were hostages.” As Russians installed their own officials and laws on occupied territories, operating an aid organization became untenable. After being ejected from Donetsk, Shybalov relocated to Kyiv. At 6 a.m. on Feb. 24, 2022, Shybalov woke up to a call from a friend. The full-scale invasion had begun. He heard fighter jets and explosions. For the next two hours, he watched the news, drank coffee and smoked one cigarette after another. By 10:30 a.m., Shybalov enlisted to fight. His sergeant handed him a rocket-propelled grenade launcher. “Congrats,” the sergeant said, “now you are our grenadier.” After helping push the Russian army back from the outskirts of Kyiv, he was deployed to the border between the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. Another Ukrainian brigade nearby withdrew, but Shybalov and his unit were not informed. It was four of them against a battalion of Russian paratroopers, he said. They were encircled after a week. After being bound, interrogated and shifted among holding facilities, Shybalov landed in a prison in Luhansk. He said he was beaten and tortured. Shybalov did not see the sun for six months and shed over 30 pounds during his captivity. “We had porridge with worms for breakfast and porridge with sand for supper,” he said. Shybalov said he was a high-value prisoner for the Russians because he was from the east, had been a journalist and worked with international organizations. They were keen to present him as an American spy, he said — a charge that carries a sentence of up to 20 years. One day, a Russian intelligence officer told Shybalov he was recording an interview with Russia Today, the government-controlled media outlet. “Prepare yourself,” the Russian said. “They will come here in five minutes.” Shybalov was invited into a comfortable room with a sofa. The crew had two iPhones. One of the men treated him cordially, offering tea and cigarettes. He spoke as if they were having a friendly chat. “Like two mates having their Friday beer and softly discussing global matters,” Shybalov said. It was different from a local crew that had come earlier and given prisoners scripts to read. The RT crew was more sophisticated. “They really manipulated you to make you say something understood as a pro-Russian position or anti-Ukrainian, but these are words said by you,” he said. “They’re just trying to manipulate you to catch you on that hook.” The intelligence officer, meanwhile, implicitly threatened to return him to his interrogators, who waited outside the door. Shybalov tried to control his gestures and his breathing during the two-hour interview. “Talking to them, I even prohibited myself from feeling something,” he said. When he returned to his cell, he did not discuss the video much. He shared the half a pack of cigarettes the Russian intelligence officer gave him with his cellmates. Back home, the video helped place him on an exchange list by adding to the evidence that he was captive rather than missing in action. His wife, Duman, filed reports with all the authorities she could think of. Unable to sleep in their shared bed while he was imprisoned, she rested on a sleeping bag on the floor and kept herself busy delivering aid to soldiers on the front line. She and her friend used to drive out onto a bridge in Kyiv, roll down their windows and scream. “That was our method to de-stress,” she said. Shybalov was not told where he was going before he was exchanged in December 2022. A Russian guard told him he was about to be executed, then said it was a joke. He arrived on Ukrainian soil and sang the Ukrainian anthem on the bus home with other prisoners. “This is what could never happen in a Russian cell, even in a dream,” he said, “that you could sing the Ukrainian anthem and not be beaten for that.” After seven months of captivity, he came home on New Year’s Eve. “I did not cry; I screamed very loudly,” Duman said of the moment she found out that he was coming home. “I think I woke up half the building.” Since his return, Shybalov and Duman relocated from Kyiv to the small town of Mykolaiv in Ukraine’s western Lviv region, where Duman is from. The couple keeps to themselves. Shybalov had heard about Volodymyr Srebrodolskyy, whose village denied him a final resting place on the land where he was born. It enraged him. “Russian propaganda — it’s an industry,” he said. “They facilitate this as an industry with the needed volume of basic raw materials, which are interrogations and interviews with prisoners of war.” All of the former prisoners Shybalov keeps in touch with have had to film them, he said. “They really perceive media as a weapon, culture as a weapon, language as a weapon and religion as a weapon,” he said. “Thus, they treat it as a proper weapon. They invest big resources to produce it. They design sophisticated and smart tactics how to use it. And they have thousands of people engaged in it.” A cell in Donetsk Volodymyr Srebrodolskyy’s captors placed him in a detention facility in Chystiakove, a city known as Torez until 2016, occupied by the Russian army since 2014. Located behind a double fence, the prison complex was built to hold 1,200 prisoners. Among them was Mykola Shustrov, an army medic captured in the southern city of Mariupol while Russia brutally besieged it in the spring of 2022. Shustrov spent nearly three years in Russian captivity being moved between holding facilities. “They came to our cell,” Shustrov remembered of one prison, “they hung up Putin’s portrait, the anthem of the Russian Federation and told us to learn it.” After forcing the prisoners to learn the words from the anthem lyrics posted in the cell, their captors told them to sing individual couplets and questioned them about how many lines it contained. If they could not answer, the prisoners would be beaten. By the time he got to Chystiakove, Shustrov’s teeth had been knocked out from repeated beatings and interrogations, and he lost a lot of weight because of the meager food rations. About a year into his captivity, a video crew arrived. Shustrov and others were brought to a room where one man questioned him while another sat off camera in a balaclava and military gear. When he entered the room, Shustrov was punched in the gut. “If you don’t want that repeated,” his captors said, “answer.” Shustrov’s interviewers were looking for compromising information on the Ukrainian army. Shustrov sat at the table, looking down, stuttering and trying to respond as neutrally as he could. The chance to show their families they’re alive was the main motivation for prisoners to cooperate with the propagandists, Shustrov said. “You will say anything to show yourself,” he said. Srebrodolskyy arrived in Shustrov’s cell in late 2024, in agony. He was badly beaten after failing to recite the Russian anthem, he told Shustrov and other cellmates. Srebrodolskyy’s stomach was swollen and tender from the assault, Shustrov remembered. His medical training made it clear how acute the situation was. “I can’t even drink water,” Srebrodolskyy told him. The men asked for a doctor, but the guards said he would have to wait until morning. Shustrov spent all night speaking with the 55-year-old to distract him from the pain. “I could not help him,” Shustrov said. “In our barracks, all I had was two hands and cold water from the tap. That’s it.” An ambulance took him away in the morning, but it was too late to save Srebrodolskyy’s life. He was not the first man Shustrov watched die in captivity. “He was in prison for the rest of his life,” Shustrov said, “and you begin to think, ‘Why am I enduring all of this?’” Shustrov, who was released in a February 2025 exchange, was indignant about the village’s reaction to Srebrodolskyy’s video. The only fact to be taken from it, he said, was that the person was alive at the time of filming. Nobody can know what the captive endured, he said. “You’re a prisoner there,” Shustrov said. “You’re not a person.” Sixty miles from home Following months of uncertainty, Srebrodolskyy was buried at the edge of a city cemetery some 60 miles from his home, away from a section housing the bodies of other service members. After his body was repatriated in April 2025, Ukraine’s Donetsk prosecutor’s office opened a criminal investigation into Srebrodolskyy’s death. An autopsy concluded he died of a stab wound to the stomach, a spokesperson said. The investigation is ongoing. The mayor of Karpylivka, Srebrodolskyy’s home village, said he saw the video but denied responsibility for the lack of local burial, declining to speak further on the topic. The plaque on Srebrodolskyy’s grave bears no date of death. A photo of his face with cavernous wrinkles sits in the center of a cross. Those who heard about his story have come by to place candles, flowers, kind notes and a Ukrainian flag that unfurls when the steppe winds blow. “I am only 55. I just want for God to give me a couple more years,” Srebrodolskyy said in his video. “To live quietly and peacefully.”

articles.title: Attacker opens fire near high school in western Turkiye, wounding 11
articles.summary: Police arrest suspect after shooting near high school; injured people rushed to local hospitals for treatment.
articles.body:
An attacker has opened fire near a high school in western Turkiye, wounding at least 11 people, authorities said.

Two of the wounded were in critical condition, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said on Tuesday morning, soon after the attack took place near a vocational and technical high school in the Turgutlu district in the western Manisa province.

The Haberturk news channel said the assailant was a student at the school.

The suspect was arrested. Their parents and grandfather, who owned the ⁠weapon used in the attack, have also been detained, Gurlek said.

The motive for the attack was not immediately clear, according to Gurlek, who said two chief prosecutors were appointed to investigate the shooting, including claims that the student was bullied at the school.

“When the security of our children is at stake, it is not possible for any negligence or irresponsibility to be overlooked,” Gurlek wrote on X.

“The circumstances under which the child obtained the gun used in the attack, the conditions of the weapon’s storage, the parents’ obligations regarding care and supervision, and allegations of bullying before the incident are being investigated thoroughly and from multiple angles,” he added.

Images and video posted online appeared to show the suspect walking along a street near the school holding a rifle before running back down the same street. Separate footage captured outside the building showed police pushing back families and onlookers gathered near the premises.

The attack comes months after two deadly school shootings shocked the country in April.

In one incident, 16 people, mostly students, were wounded when a former student opened fire at a high school in the Sanliurfa province before killing himself.

The following day, a 14-year-old killed nine people , including students and teachers, and wounded 13 others in an attack at his school in the Kahramanmaras province before being killed by the police.

Before those events, Turkiye had no history of such school attacks. The April shootings led to widespread outrage and prompted officials to introduce new security measures for the 2026-27 academic year, including tighter gun controls.

articles.title: Paramount just won its $110 billion Warner Bros battle, here's what it had to give up
articles.summary: Tech News News: Paramount Skydance has emerged victorious in its Warner Bros Discovery takeover, finalizing a $110 billion acquisition after settling lawsuits with a .
articles.body: Paramount Skydance has emerged victorious in its Warner Bros Discovery takeover, finalizing a $110 billion acquisition after settling lawsuits with a coalition of US states led by California and the Writers Guild of America, according to a report by Reuters. The deal, one of the largest in media history, consolidates power across Hollywood’s film, TV, streaming, and news businesses.To avoid a forced sale of assets like CNN or major film franchises, Paramount agreed to temporary film quotas and the creation of a news oversight committee. The company pledged to spend at least $300 million more annually on US film production, release 30–32 movies per year for five years, and ensure that at least 20% are blockbusters and four are independent films. Paramount also promised not to raise rates on theater operators for three years.Paramount CEO David Ellison on victoryParamount CEO David Ellison thanked state officials and California Governor Gavin Newsom for their support, saying: “Our goal has always been to build a stronger Hollywood — one with more stories told, greater choice for consumers and stronger competition.” The settlement also saves Paramount from paying a $7 million-a-day “ticking fee” to Warner shareholders had the deal not closed by September 30.A costly win for ParamountThe settlement marks a significant victory for Paramount CEO David Ellison, who spent months battling state regulators to finalize a deal that would dramatically consolidate power across Hollywood's film, TV, streaming, and news businesses. But the win came with strings attached. Paramount agreed to temporary film production quotas and a news oversight committee, while managing to avoid the far more damaging outcome opponents had pushed for: a forced sale of cable assets like CNN or any of its major film franchises.Markets reacted quickly. Warner Bros Discovery shares surged more than 10% on the news, delighting its shareholders, while Paramount's own stock pared back earlier gains — a sign investors see the settlement as a win overall, even if not an entirely clean one for Paramount.What Paramount had to agree toUnder the terms of the settlement, Paramount committed to spending at least $300 million more annually on domestic film production and to sticking to US theatrical release quotas for five years. Specifically, the company will produce 30 movies in each of the first two years of the deal, rising to 32 movies annually for the following three years. Of those, at least four films per year must be independent productions, and at least 20% must be blockbusters — if Paramount misses that mark, it will owe $30 million per film short, with most of that money funneled into funds supporting industry workers.Paramount also agreed not to raise rates on theater operators for three years, and will set up a dedicated news editorial independence board to safeguard journalistic independence at CBS and CNN.Writers Guild settles, but stays criticalThe Writers Guild of America settled its own parallel lawsuit against Paramount as part of the broader resolution, though the union made clear it still believes the merger will ultimately harm the industry. With the states' settlement in place, the union was left to weigh continuing the fight alone, without government backing, in a case that would have cost millions of dollars to pursue independently.California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the states' case, described the outcome as a strong antitrust result, emphasizing that the resolution wasn't about blocking the merger itself but about securing more production, more choice, and competitive guardrails for the industry — reiterating that he still doesn't believe the two companies should have merged in the first place.What's still at stakeThe companies have previously said the merger is expected to generate $6 billion in savings, largely through cost cuts likely to affect jobs across Hollywood, including at CNN and CBS. The combined entity is expected to carry roughly $80 billion in debt once the deal closes.The timing of the settlement also carries real financial weight: it allows Paramount to avoid a $7 million-a-day "ticking fee" it would have owed Warner Bros Discovery shareholders for every day the deal remained unclosed past September 30. With antitrust regulators in the European Union and Britain having already cleared the deal, Monday's settlement removes one of the last major roadblocks standing between Paramount and closing the largest media merger in years.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Path to Scotland's first Center Parcs near Hawick secures funding support
articles.summary: The funding will help with the design costs for a potential £12m path between Hawick and Selkirk.
articles.body:
A proposed £12m path linking two towns in the Borders to Scotland's first Center Parcs has secured funding support.

The aim is to cut car journeys and increase active travel, with daily commuting trips between Hawick and Selkirk expected to more than double when the holiday village opens in 2029.

It is one of a range or projects in the region to have gained nearly £3.5m of Transport Scotland funding.

Jenny Linehan, executive member for transport on Scottish Borders Council, said it was a "significant" award which could help make active travel a "realistic and attractive choice for more people".

The £12m path to Scotland's first Center Parcs - practical or pricey?

Path could link two towns ahead of Center Parcs opening

Consultation on the plans was held earlier this year.

The project - to run near the route of the A7 - has divided opinion with some people describing it as a "great idea" but others considering the price "excessive".

Concerns have been raised about how many people would want to walk on a path next to a busy road and some residents have suggested upgrading the existing Abbey Way would be a better option.

However, others in the area have backed the plans and called for an extended path network across the region.

Scottish Borders Council has estimated that if the path was built there could be more than 200 daily cycling trips to and from Center Parcs made by staff and visitors.

A project timeline could firstly see the section from Hawick to the holiday village built around the time the park opens in 2029, with the second section to Selkirk being constructed after that.

The path project is one of a number to have secured backing for either their design or construction.

All work on the projects is expected to be completed by 31 March next year.

Jenny Linehan said the projects would help improve the links between towns and villages and make active travel more straightforward.

Transport Secretary Steven Flynn added: "Projects like these help connect communities, support healthier lifestyles, strengthen local economies and encourage more sustainable travel choices for residents and visitors alike."
