articles.title: From punk to politics - the making of new Reform Wales leader Helen Jenner
articles.summary: Who is Reform's new Welsh leader, former English teacher Helen Jenner?
articles.body:
Helen Jenner, the new leader of Reform Wales, got a taster session for the top job on Tuesday, with a confident performance quizzing Plaid Cymru First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth in the Senedd.

The Bangor Conwy Môn MS took over after her predecessor Dan Thomas quit as leader following an arrest on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

As an ex-teacher, Jenner reckons she has no fears appearing before politicians in Cardiff Bay.

Over the summer she told the BBC Walescast podcast it was "nothing compared to year 11 last lesson on a Friday".

"You can't get a more discerning audience than a class of teenagers," she said.

There's a smattering of showbiz glitz in Jenner's background.

She taught English at the Brit School for the performing arts in south London, where Adele and Amy Winehouse studied.

Her pupils included Britain's Got Talent semi-finalist Harrison Pettman.

Reform not suspending former leader arrested on suspicion of assault, says chief whip

Reform defector reveals she voted Remain in Brexit vote and wants Welsh independence

Born in Neath, where her mother is from, Jenner moved to Anglesey aged two where she learned Welsh at school.

She studied English literature at Bangor University.

With bright, pink hair, she was more focused on singing in a "very punk, rocky type" band called The Mephs, short for Mephistophelean Engines of Pleasure.

It is not, one suspects, the sort of name dreamt up by someone planning a future career in Welsh politics. Indeed, she says politics was not something she was into then.

"My dad banging on about the European Union constantly," she said.

Her father, who's from Liverpool, had joined UKIP. Then Jenner saw Nigel Farage on television.

"It was seeing him, and then watching his YouTube clips in the European Parliament and everything: I've never seen anybody so animated," said Jenner.

"I felt he was really principled and I suddenly thought 'oh, I actually care about politics now'."

She became a fellow UKIP member and stood for Nigel Farage's next party, the Brexit Party at the 2019 UK general election.

Married with two children, Jenner describes herself as a "proud British person" but "first and foremost" a "very proud Welsh person".

Reform is by far the biggest opposition party Cardiff Bay has seen, albeit with its seat tally dropping to 33 after a defection to Plaid Cymru last week.

After a tumultuous week for Reform, Jenner's first job is damage limitation.

Her second, longer-term task, is convincing Welsh voters that Reform is more than Nigel Farage's party in Wales and has the makings of the next Welsh government.

articles.summary: US News: Discover the transformation of Falcon Lair, a Beverly Hills estate previously owned by silent-film star Rudolph Valentino. New owners plan a 17,000-square-foot modern mansion, adding a new chapter to this iconic property’s history.
articles.body: A four-acre Beverly Hills estate with ties to silent-film star Rudolph Valentino is set for another transformation. According to the New York Post, the property, known as Falcon Lair, was purchased for $15 million in 2021 by a Beverly Hills business couple, after the historic mansion that once stood there had already been demolished. The owners later drew up plans for a new 17,000-square-foot residence, adding another chapter to the property’s Hollywood history.Rudolph Valentino's Falcon LairAccording to Forbes, Falcon Lair’s best-known chapter began in 1925, when Italian-born actor Rudolph Valentino bought the Beverly Hills property for $175,000. Valentino was one of the biggest stars of the silent-film era, known for films including The Sheikh and Blood and Sand. He named the estate Falcon Lair after The Hooded Falcon, a film project he had planned but never completed. The property became a private retreat that reflected Valentino’s interest in European-style architecture and furnishings.The main house was an 11-bedroom Mediterranean-style villa. It was designed by architect Wallace Neff. The star furnished the house with antique furniture. There were gardens, stables, and even places where he kept his Arabian horses and falcons. The house formed part of the star’s public image. Valentino’s stay at Falcon Lair was brief. He passed away in August 1926 at the age of 31, barely less than two years after purchasing the land. The estate went through a series of transfers after his death before it was eventually linked to tobacco heiress Doris Duke.The mansion disappearsA major turning point came in 2006, when Valentino’s old house was demolished. The demolition mattered because the house had been a central part of Falcon Lair, and once it was gone, no main residence remained on the property. However, there remained many historical parts of this property, such as the caretaker’s house, two-car garage, and even some landscaped areas. A historic entrance with pillars and crests also remained.The site was later divided and sold in separate parcels. In 2020, the couple who would eventually acquire the larger estate purchased a 1.25-acre portion for $3.75 million, according to Architectural Digest. A year later, they bought the four-acre property for $15 million, bringing together the land on which a new estate could be developed. The transactions show that historic celebrity properties can retain value even after the original buildings are gone. In Falcon Lair's case, the name, location, surviving features and association with Valentino and Duke continued to form part of the property's identity.A 17,000-square-foot replacementThe owners who acquired Falcon Lair in 2021 rejected reconstructing the demolished house and instead developed plans for a much larger modern home of up to 17,000 square feet. The home was designed by Appleton Partners, with interiors by Mark D. Sikes. Rather than reconstructing the Wallace Neff villa, the proposed design takes a very different approach while still acknowledging the site's history.Those plans became a major selling point when Falcon Lair was listed for $10.99 million in November 2025. The sale included the approved plans for the future home, giving potential buyers the option to acquire the property with a ready development plan. The asking price was well below the $15 million paid for the four-acre plot in 2021. Falcon Lair therefore stood at the junction of two periods, nearly a century after Valentino immortalised the place with his name. If the approved plans are carried forward by a future owner, the new structure would be much larger than Valentino's villa.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: To Kill a Mockingbird first edition found in London Oxfam shop
articles.summary: An original US edition of To Kill a Mockingbird is found in an Oxfam store in west London.
articles.body:
A rare first edition of the novel To Kill A Mockingbird has been found among items donated to Oxfam, according to the charity.

The copy of Harper Lee's seminal 1960 work was discovered in a box of American books given to the charity's bookshop in Portobello Road, west London.

It has since been acquired by the British Library and will join its national collection.

Shop manager Olivia Haysman-Walker, who identified the copy as being a first US edition, said the book could easily have been missed. "There were lots of books to work through in the donation, but we recognised To Kill A Mockingbird and thought it was worth taking a closer look."

She added: "We realised quite quickly that we had something really special.

"The dust jacket showed its age, and although it was worn around the edges, the pages inside were in beautiful condition.

"It's amazing to think that this book has passed through our Oxfam bookshop and into the national collection at the British Library.

"It really has been quite a journey, and it's a lovely reminder, during Second Hand September, of the kind of treasures that can be hiding among the shelves and donations in our shops."

Second Hand September is Oxfam's annual campaign encouraging people to buy second-hand.

Lee's Pulitzer Prize-winning book tells the story of lawyer Atticus Finch as he defends Tom Robinson, a black man wrongly accused of raping a white woman.

Her story of racial injustice and childhood innocence, set in Alabama in 1934, has sold more than 40 million copies around the world and has been translated into 40 languages.

The US novelist, who was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, died in 2016 at the age of 89.

articles.title: Why United Nations says US boat strikes may be ‘crimes against humanity’
articles.summary: Washington justifies the attacks as necessary to halt the flow of lethal drugs into the US.
articles.body:
A United Nations report has concluded that US strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific are illegal and could constitute “crimes against humanity”.

In a report published on Monday, UN Special Rapporteur Ben Saul said attacks on 68 vessels from September last year to August killed at least 223 people and entailed the “illegal use” of disproportionate force.

The findings were released just days after the US military announced its latest attack on another boat, which killed four people. US President Donald Trump’s administration, which frames the operations against the boats as part of a military conflict, said they are necessary to prevent the flow of lethal drugs into the United States. It has described the drug shipments as an “armed attack” on US territory.

Here’s what we know about why the US has been attacking the boats and whether these strikes are legal:

The report found that the strikes by US forces are unjustified under national and international law and thus amount to “serial extrajudicial killings in violation of the right to life”.

They “plausibly constitute crimes against humanity”, it said.

Even if those attacked were found to be members of organised criminal or “terrorist” groups as the US has claimed, there is no evidence that they had launched an armed attack on the US or were being used as proxies by other countries, which would warrant a US military attack, the report noted.

Saul, the UN special rapporteur on counterterrorism and human rights, added that drug trafficking “is not equivalent to a military attack”.

Furthermore, observers have noted , the Trump administration has never provided any evidence that any of the boats it has struck were trafficking drugs.

The UN report also cast doubt over the legality of the US abduction of former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January, during which 75 people were killed, as well as collaborations with other Latin American countries under the Trump administration-initiated “Shield of the Americas”. The initiative seeks to extend US antidrug operations to land across the region.

The UN report called for internal investigations and for commanders involved in the operations to be held accountable.

It concluded that the strikes have failed to prevent the arrival of cocaine in the US on container ships. which are not adequately checked.

Why has the US launched strikes on boats?

Washington first began striking boats it claimed were trafficking drugs from Venezuela to the US across the Eastern Pacific and Caribbean in September last year.

The US military has routinely released videos on social media showing the moments the vessels are hit but has disclosed little about those killed and has not provided evidence tying them to drug trafficking.

Furthermore, experts said most drugs come into the US via Mexico by land through its southern border and do not originate in Venezuela. Families of those killed have often said they were fishermen and not drug smugglers.

The UN report listed 223 casualties from 68 strikes carried out through August.

Two additional attacks this month have raised the number of those killed to 234 in 70 strikes.

In the first set of attacks on September 2, 2025, the US military allegedly used a “ double tap ” tactic, launching a second attack to finish off the survivors of an initial strike. The first attacks killed 11 people.

The move drew intense criticism from the US Congress, which called for the Pentagon to release full videos of the strikes.

There were also allegations that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had given the order to “kill them all” in the double-tap strike. However, senior military commanders later testified in Congress that he did not.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Michael Vigil, former chief of international operations at the US Drug Enforcement Administration, said: “That is murder. No matter how you spell it out, it’s murder, … and it shocks the moral conscience.”

The most recent attack on Saturday killed four people, according to the US military. It alleged that the boat was travelling “along established narco-trafficking routes” and “confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking”.

Trump has claimed the US is in an “armed conflict” with drug cartels and has repeatedly justified the boat attacks as necessary to halt the flow of drugs into the country.

Senior officials have also claimed the US is abiding by due process. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a Senate hearing in July that “every strike has a legal officer on the deck that has to make a determination about whether the call is legal or not”.

Rights organisations, however, have challenged the killings. In January, the families of two Trinidadian men – Chad Joseph, 26, and Rishi Samaroo, 41 – brought the first case against the US government over the boat attacks to a federal court in Massachusetts. The suit, aided by US legal groups, argued the victims were fishermen.

Separately in December, the family of Colombian Alejandro Carranza Medina filed a human rights complaint with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, which is part of the Organization of American States.

Can any action be taken against US officials?

The term “crimes against humanity” implies that killings have been carried out systematically in accordance with a plan by a state or an organised group and are an especially serious crime.

Perpetrators accused of such crimes can be tried and convicted only before the International Criminal Court (ICC), which examines whether those carrying out attacks were aware that their actions targeted a civilian population and whether their actions resulted in the killing of multiple people.

US courts cannot try such cases because no specific federal laws criminalise crimes against humanity.

The US is not a member of the ICC, and no American has been tried before the court in The Hague.

The Trump administration has been hostile to the ICC because of arrest warrants issued for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. The US has complained the court is targeting officials from non-ICC countries.

Washington has sanctioned more than a dozen ICC judges and prosecutors since February last year and is reportedly preparing more sanctions against the court itself.

articles.title: Hurricane Polo grows into a Category 4 storm in the Pacific off Mexico
articles.summary: Hurricane Polo grew into a Category 4 storm in the eastern Pacific late on Monday and was forecast to bring heavy rain to southwestern Mexico but remain offshore.
articles.body: MIAMI — Hurricane Polo grew into a Category 4 storm in the eastern Pacific late on Monday and was forecast to bring heavy rain to southwestern Mexico but remain offshore. It had maximum sustained winds of 130 mph (215 kph) and may intensify further and reach Category 5 strength Tuesday or Wednesday, the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said. Category 4 storms have winds of 130-156 mph (210-250 kph) on the Saffir-Simpson scale, and Category 5 hurricanes have winds exceeding 157 mph (250 kph). Polo was moving east-southeast at 5 mph (7 kph) and was forecast to sharply turn northwest and west-northwest. On that path, Polo would skirt the Mexican coast for a few days without directly making landfall. A tropical storm watch was issued for part of the coast south of Manzanillo in Colima state to Tecpan de Galeana in Guerrero state, meaning tropical storm conditions were possible in the area within two days. Polo was centered about 330 miles (530 kilometers) south-southeast of Manzanillo as of late Monday. Heavy rain with the potential for flooding and landslides was forecast for coastal Guerrero and Michoacán states through Thursday. Smaller amounts of rain were possible in coastal portions of Oaxaca, Colima and Jalisco states. Farther west in the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Odalys was far from land but expected to become a hurricane by midweek. Odalys had maximum sustained winds of 50 mph (85 kph) on Monday. In the Atlantic Ocean, Tropical Storm Fay had weakened to 40 mph (65 kph) southwest of the Azores and was forecast to be a remnant low by late Tuesday. No Atlantic hurricanes have formed yet this year, and this year has set a record for the longest a season has begun without a hurricane. The effects of this year’s El Nino crush storms before they get going.

articles.title: The Revisit: 125 shells, 10 minutes and a German attack on Madras - when WWI reached India
articles.summary: India News: When World War I broke out in Europe in July 1914, Madras was thousands of kilometres away from the battlefields. Yet there was little certainty among.
articles.body: When World War I broke out in Europe in July 1914, Madras was thousands of kilometres away from the battlefields. Yet there was little certainty among British authorities that the war would remain confined to Europe. The city's strategic importance as a major port made it vulnerable, and within weeks, residents were being advised to move towards safer places in the hinterland.By September, the anxiety had become real enough for some families to leave.Among them were the grandparents of PD Balaji, professor and head of the department of ancient history and archaeology at the University of Madras. Speaking to The Times of India in 2017, Balaji recalled that his grandparents lived in Royapettah and moved to Salem briefly, taking some valuables with them because they feared Madras could come under attack.Their fears were realised on the night of September 22, 1914, when the German cruiser SMS Emden appeared off the Madras coast and opened fire.The attack lasted only a short time, but it became one of the most remarkable episodes of India's experience of World War I.The warship that did not look GermanThe Emden had already been operating in the waters around the Indian subcontinent, attacking shipping before turning towards Madras. But the cruiser had an unusual advantage: it did not necessarily look like an enemy vessel from a distance.Historian Venkatesh Ramakrishnan told TOI that the Emden had a dummy fourth funnel, which made the German cruiser appear like a British ship.That deception was particularly useful in the busy waters of the region."Some enemy ships even saluted it during navigation," Ramakrishnan told TOI.The disguise allowed the cruiser to move through waters where a genuine German warship might otherwise have attracted immediate attention. By the time it approached Madras, the British authorities were facing a vessel that had managed to exploit both surprise and confusion.130 shells in one nightAt around 9.30 pm, the attack began.The precise nature of the German target remains one of the interesting questions surrounding the bombardment. Some accounts have suggested that Fort St George was the intended target, while historian Venkatesh Ramakrishnan offered a different explanation.According to Ramakrishnan, Captain Karl von Müller did not necessarily direct his guns at one particular building."The Emden's captain Karl von Muller did not aim at any particular target. The shells were fired on any structure that was illuminated by the lighthouse," he told TOI.Around 130 shells were fired that night, according to Ramakrishnan.One struck a storage tank belonging to the Burmah Oil Company near the harbour. The tank caught fire, and the blaze continued for three days, turning the attack into a highly visible spectacle for the city.A separate 2014 TOI report, quoting historian V Dhivakar, put the number of shells at at least 125, fired within around 10 minutes. Dhivakar said the shells hit oil tanks containing approximately 350,000 gallons of oil.Whatever the precise count, the scale of the bombardment was remarkable for an attack that lasted only a short period.The German cruiser had sailed close enough to Madras to fire into the city and then withdrew before the British could mount an effective response.From harbour to high courtThe attack was not confined to the waterfront.According to Ramakrishnan, shrapnel struck several parts of Madras, including the High Court, General Hospital, Vepery, Haddows Road, Poonamallee High Road, the gun battery at Royapuram, Casa Major Road and George Town.The geography of the damage is significant because it demonstrated how a naval attack on the harbour could quickly become a city-wide shock.For residents, the source of the explosions was initially not something they could easily understand. The war had until then existed largely in newspapers and official announcements. Suddenly, its sound could be heard across Madras.And the sight of the oil tank burning for days provided a lasting reminder that the British Empire's war had reached the Indian coast.A city already preparing to fleeThe Emden attack did not come completely out of the blue.Anxiety had spread through Madras in the weeks following the outbreak of World War I. British authorities had advised residents to move to safer locations in the hinterland because of fears that enemy forces could attack the city.The exodus had already begun when the German cruiser struck.For families who had left, the decision suddenly appeared prescient. For those who remained, the bombardment reinforced fears that the Emden might return or that other German vessels could attack the city.The account of Balaji's grandparents provides a glimpse into what that uncertainty meant at an individual level. They left their Royapettah home for Salem and carried valuables with them, not knowing how long they would have to stay away.This was not merely a military episode. It had begun affecting ordinary civilian decisions.Why did Emden leave?The attack also produced a question that historians continue to debate: Why did the Emden withdraw so quickly?The cruiser had managed to reach Madras, fire more than a hundred shells and hit important infrastructure. Yet it did not remain to inflict prolonged damage.Historian V Dhivakar challenged the later British explanation that Emden withdrew because of the British response.“After Emden reached a safe distance, the British started responding towards what for them was an unknown object in the dark far out at sea,” Dhivakar told TOI.He argued that the German cruiser could potentially have inflicted considerably more damage had it remained longer.The question becomes more intriguing when the Emden's capabilities are considered. Dhivakar described the cruiser as a formidable warship for its time, armed with ten 10.5cm guns and two torpedo tubes.Why Muller chose to stop when he did remains one of the enduring mysteries of the Madras raid.The Emden story also acquired an Indian revolutionary dimension through Chempakaraman Pillai, an Indian-born political activist and revolutionary who was living in Germany.A persistent claim has suggested that Pillai helped the Germans plan the Madras attack or was aboard the Emden.But the evidence cited by Dhivakar does not establish that.He told TOI that Pillai was not aboard the Emden during its wartime operations. Dhivakar referred to a book by Hellmuth von Mucke, the ship's vice-commander, which recorded several incidents aboard the cruiser without mentioning Pillai.Mucke did, however, refer to an Indian passenger who provided information.That detail has helped keep the Indian connection alive, but it does not prove that Pillai himself was involved in the attack.The word 'Emden' survivesThe most curious legacy of the raid may have been linguistic.The name Emden became part of popular usage in southern India, particularly in Tamil, where it came to be associated with someone formidable, daring or intimidating.The German cruiser therefore outlived its own military career in an unexpected way.The ship was eventually cornered and destroyed later in 1914, but its name had already acquired a place in Indian memory.For Madras, meanwhile, the physical reminders of the bombardment became part of the city's history. The High Court was among the places struck by shrapnel, while accounts of the attack have continued to document the damage caused across the harbour and surrounding neighbourhoods.The night war came homeThe Emden attack did not change the outcome of World War I. It did not result in the capture of Madras, nor did it lead to a prolonged German campaign on the Indian coast.Its significance was different.It showed that a war that seemed distant and European could reach an Indian city with little warning. It exposed the vulnerability of a major colonial port, sent residents fleeing towards the interior and forced the British to confront the possibility that India's coastline could become part of the global conflict.For the people of Madras, September 22, 1914, was therefore not simply another date in the history of World War I.It was the night when the distant war suddenly became local: when a German cruiser appeared off the coast, 130 shells tore into the city, a Burmah Oil tank burned for three days, shrapnel reached the High Court and other parts of Madras, and a word that once belonged to a German warship entered the vocabulary of southern India.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Fat Bear Week opens for Alaska’s heavyweight crown. Can Chunk, the 1,200-pound champ, win again?
articles.summary: After a summer spent packing away sockeye salmon, Alaska’s heftiest brown bears are ready to throw their weight around.
articles.body: ANCHORAGE, Alaska — After a summer spent packing away sockeye salmon, Alaska’s heftiest brown bears are ready to throw their weight around. Online voting began Tuesday for Fat Bear Week, the annual contest that pits the rotund residents of Katmai National Park and Preserve against each other for the title of most oversized ursine. Last year’s winner, Chunk — known officially as Bear 32 — is hungry for a repeat. Chunk’s weight in 2025 was estimated at 1,200 pounds, which gave him a narrow victory. This year he’s back and facing corpulent competition like Gully — aka Bear 903 — the offspring of two-time champion Grazer. The contest, which is in its 12th year, celebrates the resilience of the 2,200 brown bears that live in the preserve on the Alaska Peninsula, which extends from the state’s southwest corner toward the Aleutian Islands. The animals gorge on the abundant salmon that return to the Brooks River, sometimes chomping the fish in midair as they make their way upstream to spawn. The event this year features 16 bears facing off in a single-elimination, bracket-style tournament. All voting is done online at with the winner declared Sept. 29. The public can watch the bears on explore.org’s livestream cameras before deciding on their favorite. “Fat bears are successful bears,” the nonprofit’s website says. They gorge on salmon starting in late June in order to accumulate fat reserves to prepare for winter hibernation, when they do not eat or drink and lose one-third of their body weight. Adult male brown bears typically weigh 600 to 900 pounds (about 270 to 410 kilograms) in midsummer. By the time they are ready to hibernate after feasting on migrating and spawning salmon — each eats as many as 30 fish per day — large males can weigh well over 1,000 pounds (454 kilograms). Females are about one-third smaller. Voters in the online contest can review before-and-after photos of the bears, lean at the start of summer and fattened at the end. The bears are not actually weighed — imagine that process — and some fans choose their favorite based on their looks or backstory. To be featured in the contest, the bears must frequent the area around the river. The live cameras at Brooks Falls captured the moments in 2024 when mother bear 128 Grazer ’s cub slipped over the waterfall and floated into the fishing spot occupied by Chunk, who attacked and injured the cub. Grazer fought Chunk, but the cub ultimately died. After the dramatic fight, voting fans handed Grazer a victory over Chunk. Then Chunk returned in 2025 to take the title. Fat Bear Week was started in 2014 as an interactive way to inform the public about brown bears, the coastal cousins of grizzlies.

articles.title: A weathered Wyoming cabin used as a storage shed turned out to be a 140-year-old Chinese laundry; after an eight-year rescue effort, the building has been moved to a museum for restoration
articles.summary: US News: A weathered cabin that spent decades being used as a storage shed behind a building on Main Street in Lander, Wyoming, has been identified as a late 1.
articles.body: A weathered cabin that spent decades being used as a storage shed behind a building on Main Street in Lander, Wyoming, has been identified as a late 19th-century Chinese laundry and bathhouse. The building belonged to Sam Sing, one of Lander’s early and influential residents.The small log cabin was donated to the Fremont County Pioneer Museum about eight years ago by property owner Tony McRae. The donation began a long effort to raise money, move the structure and preserve it. The building has now been moved to the museum’s Pioneer Village, where it will be restored and turned into an exhibit.Sing was among about 30 Chinese residents living in the town, which had a population of around 1,000 at the time. Historical records describe the Chinese residents as important contributors to the growing community, although they also faced restrictions, discrimination and hostility.Museum Director Randy Wise said Sing played a role in improving Lander. One example was his support for concrete sidewalks at a time when many Western towns relied on wooden boardwalks. According to Wise, “Sing said we, as a developing community, needed these. We needed to keep improving the community. So he was very interested in helping the community grow.”How Sam Sing went from gold fields to laundrySing was born Sing Yee Wind in Canton Province, China, in 1859. He later travelled to America, where he worked in California’s gold fields. He eventually went to South Pass City in Wyoming, joining others hoping to make money from the mining boom there.The boom did not last long, and Sing later moved to Lander. He worked as a cook at the Lander Hotel while continuing to look for gold and other valuable minerals. His training as a geologist also helped him recognise areas around Lander that had oil and gas deposits.Sing bought several valuable claims after recognising the potential of those deposits. However, he did not depend entirely on speculation. After saving enough money from his work at the hotel, he started a laundry and bathhouse in the small log cabin that has now been moved to the museum.The business provided services that were difficult and time-consuming for many households at the time. Laundry could require people to carry large amounts of water, cut wood, boil heavy pots and scrub clothes on metal washboards using lye.Bathing was also not as simple as it is today because many homes did not have running water. Sing could therefore earn money by providing baths, using tubs, soap, water and wood to heat it.Baths cost 25 cents in 1903Early advertisements show that Sing offered baths seven days a week for 25 cents each in 1903. The price later increased to 40 cents.His laundry and bathhouse originally stood on Main Street. It was later moved to the back of the McRae Pharmacy lot, where it remained for decades.That location may have helped save the building. It eventually became little more than a storage shed and attracted little attention. When McRae sold the main part of his business lot to Gannett Peak Sports, he still had items stored inside the old building and kept it where it was.“He was using the laundry as a storage shed, basically,” Wise said. “So nobody really paid much attention to it.”McRae eventually cleared the building and recognised its historical importance. About eight years ago, he approached the museum about taking it over. The museum agreed, but moving the old structure required money for both the relocation and a new concrete pad.The Lander Ambassadors raised just over $20,000 for that stage of the project. The historic cabin has now reached its new home at Pioneer Village.Restoration work still remainsThe building needs considerable work before it can become a museum exhibit. Some of the logs near the ground have rotted and will need to be replaced. The chinking between the logs also needs to be renewed, while the roof will be inspected to see whether repairs are required.Once the building is made weather-tight, the museum plans to replace bay doors that were added later. They will be replaced with a single door and a window on each side, which Wise said would be more historically accurate.The museum does not yet have photographs showing exactly what Sing’s laundry looked like when it was operating. If no original photographs are found, the restoration will have to be based on what an 1800s laundry in Lander would have looked like.The museum already has some original items from Sing’s laundry, along with other objects from the period. These include a working water pump. Wise said the building was close to Dickinson Creek, which runs through Lander, so Sing probably collected much of his water from the creek and may also have used a hand pump.Preserving Sing’s storyThe move has also given Pioneer Village a way to tell the story of Lander’s early Chinese residents. The village has around a dozen buildings preserving different parts of the town’s history, but this is the first building there connected to the Chinese community.Sing faced discrimination despite his standing in the community. Some children mocked him for his broken English and Chinese clothing, while he was robbed more than once. The windows of his laundry were also frequently broken by vandals.Despite those experiences, Sing remained in Lander and worked to improve the community. He never married and had no children. When he died on July 4, 1926, his brother travelled from Canton, buried him and returned to China. Sing’s headstone at Mount Hope Cemetery carries his Chinese name and an inscription in Chinese script.Wise expects the restoration of the laundry to take about a year and said more fundraising will be needed. The immediate focus is on protecting the structure from the weather.“There’s an argument to be made that moving a historic building kind of degrades its integrity,” Wise said. “I understand that argument. But the building probably would not have survived.”He added, “The building will be safe here for many, many decades so people can learn another little part of Lander history.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Why the world should care about the far right’s rise in Germany
articles.summary: The AfD has a far different vision on support for Ukraine, foreign aid and Russia than the governing coalition.
articles.body:
The Alternative fur Deutschland (AfD) party won 43.8 percent of the popular vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, trouncing the governing Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

That victory brought a party which follows in the historical footsteps of Adolf Hitler’s Nazi party closer than it has ever come since World War II to ruling a German state.

Two weeks later, the AfD took more than 38 percent of the vote in a regional election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where the Christian Democrats failed to cross the 5 percent threshold to enter the regional parliament – “a disaster”, said Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

“What it’s doing is what the far right has done elsewhere, and that is essentially erode the consensus against a set of mainstream political parties… hollowing out of the centre,” Catherine Fieschi, a political scientist with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace and an expert on the European far right, told Al Jazeera.

The left-wing Die Linke party took 25.3 percent of the vote in a separate by-election in Berlin on Sunday, illustrating how German voters are being pulled by both ends of the political spectrum.

Here’s why the far right’s rise in Germany matters to the rest of the world:

Could the far right derail German foreign policy?

Fieschi expects immediate effects on German policy towards Ukraine, which relies heavily on German financial and military industrial might.

“This is bad news for Merz. It’s bad news for Germany, and it’s bad news for the Franco-German engine, and therefore for Ukraine,” Fieschi said.

Germany’s AfD wants dialogue with Russia.

On Tuesday, as Merz’s future looked uncertain, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov lauded the AfD as a popular political force talking about “establishing relations” with Russia. “This can’t fail to appeal to us,” he said.

Ronald Meinardus, research fellow at the Hellenic Foundation for European and Foreign Policy (ELIAMEP), explained how the AfD has adopted Russian positions.

“The AfD repeatedly says they want to stop all military and financial support to Ukraine, to refuse Ukraine entry into the EU and NATO, to restore relations with Russia and restart Nord Stream .”

Europe boycotted Russian oil in 2023 in retaliation for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and will stop importing Russian gas by the end of 2027.

On Monday, Moscow reinforced the argument that dependence on Russian gas is good for Germany.

“The decline in the competitiveness of the German economy is largely due to Germany’s decision to stop buying cheap Russian gas and instead purchase much more expensive gas from other countries, primarily the United States, at times paying several times more on the spot market,” Peskov said.

There was unexpected good news for the German economy on the same day, when the country’s leading business newspaper, Handelsblatt, reported a growth forecast of 1.3 percent for 2026 – double what was previously expected.

The inward-looking AfD wants to prioritise spending for Germans, and is against foreign aid in any form.

Does the AfD have the power to set policy?

It will struggle to govern even the two states where it has a relative majority, since most other parties have ruled out working with it, and a national election is not due until early 2029.

Yet its victories put psychological pressure on the Merz government now, said Fieschi.

“Given that Merz has cancelled all his commitments, not gone to [the United Nations General Assembly in] New York, he’s going to go from crisis meeting to crisis meeting,” she said. “Merz is going to be a less effective chancellor.

“Germany is not going to stop supporting Ukraine, but I do think that it will do so even more by stealth,” said Fieschi. “I can’t see Merz getting on a train and going to Kyiv at this point.”

Oleksandr Danylyuk, an expert in Russian hybrid warfare, is even more pessimistic.

“[Moscow’s] task is to exhaust Ukraine, and to disrupt support from the West to Ukraine, and they have great progress in this regard,” Danylyuk told Al Jazeera.

“So that’s why they are confident that they can win. That’s why they’re not interested in any negotiations or ceasefire whatever, because actually, the political situation in Europe, in the US, is not optimistic at all,” said Danylyuk, who has served as a senior adviser to Ukraine’s defence minister, its foreign intelligence service and its commander-in-chief.

“Europe is going to be divided,” he predicted. “Most probably, it will not have any consensus or even keep financial support to Ukraine on the level it is right now, which is not actually enough anyhow.”

Merz came to power suggesting he might send Ukraine some of the powerful Taurus cruise missiles Germany possesses. That now seems highly unlikely.

Nor is Europe likely to resume discussion of lending Ukraine more than 200 billion euros ($230bn) in immobilised Russian money in the European financial system. That would be a game-changer, financing Ukraine’s war machine for years.

“There’s absolutely no appetite for it,” said Fieschi, citing objections from Belgium, whose depository Euroclear holds the bulk of the funds. “Loads of people are hiding behind the Belgian objection.”

The mainstream has found ways to adapt to the rise of the AfD, which took 20.8 percent of the national vote in the last general election in February 2025, twice its 2021 showing.

The CDU formed a grand coalition with their traditional ideological opponents, the Social Democrats (SPD), to keep the AfD out of national power.

Fieschi now sees Merz as a wounded animal, limping to the next round of regional elections in April 2027.

“If those elections are as bad as these, then my sense is that we could be seeing a German election in the fall of 2027.”

Could the AfD win power at the national level?

The parliamentary system makes that unlikely, said Meinardus of ELIAMEP.

“It’s very difficult for AfD to take power in the German federal system because you have several states they would have to win, and objectively cannot because they are not equally popular everywhere, and because no one will work with them,” said Meinardus.

Germany also has a powerful judiciary, which would likely challenge any unconstitutional laws the AfD tried to enact.

Protest marches against the AfD across 20 German cities on September 12 served as a reminder that the far-right party remains deeply unpopular and divisive outside its former East German power base.

articles.title: Russia and Ukraine trade deadly strikes as Zelenskyy prepares to meet with Trump
articles.summary: Russia bombarded at least four Ukrainian regions overnight with missiles and drones, killing four people, officials said Tuesday, and Ukraine’s forces damaged another Russian oil refinery in their latest long-range strike.
articles.body: Russia bombarded at least four Ukrainian regions overnight with missiles and drones, killing four people, officials said Tuesday, and Ukraine’s forces damaged another Russian oil refinery in their latest long-range strike. The ongoing exchange of daily aerial attacks, while positions on the battlefield’s front line barely change, provided a backdrop to the visit by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to the United States. Zelenskyy was due to meet other world leaders, including U.S. President Donald Trump, at the U.N. General Assembly in New York. The Ukrainian leader is hoping to recruit their help to end Russia’s more than 4½-year-old full-scale invasion of his country. Russian President Vladimir Putin isn’t due to attend the annual event. The war, which Western officials say has killed more than 500,000 Russian troops, has had global repercussions. The repeated attacks on Russian refineries, following Moscow’s strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, have caused international shortages of diesel and price spikes, according to Trump. However, the global crunch also came after the Iran war led to curtailed oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. Zelenskyy also wants help to ensure the flow of Ukrainian grain and other farm products to world markets through the Black Sea. Russian attacks on cargo vessels have severely disrupted Kyiv’s exports, hurting its economy and threatening global supplies. French President Emmanuel Macron said Tuesday that his country would provide Ukraine with more radars to help protect its power grid. He said on social media that he discussed with Trump the possibility of a truce between Moscow and Kyiv on strikes on energy infrastructure and a “moratorium” on Black Sea attacks. Zelenskyy began his New York visit by meeting with U.S. senators, thanking them for what he called strong bipartisan support for Ukraine and for recently passing a tougher Russian sanctions bill that Trump has signed into law. Peace and security will be closer once the bill is fully implemented, he said. Zelenskyy said on social media that he briefed senators on his proposals for de-escalation measures that he intends to discuss with Trump later Tuesday. The Ukrainian leader also plans to again press Trump to send more U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems that Kyiv desperately needs to stop Russia’s ballistic missiles. Ukraine said that it struck the Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara, southeast of Moscow, in an overnight attack. Several drones hit their targets, sparking a large fire at the facility, according to a statement from Ukrainian special forces. The refinery, owned by Rosneft, is a key fuel supplier for central Russia, producing gasoline, diesel, fuel oil and other petroleum products, the statement said. Ukraine said that it struck the same refinery last June. One person was killed and four others were wounded in the Samara attack, regional Gov. Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said. He said that “the enemy targeted industrial facilities,” but didn’t specify which ones. The Russian Defense Ministry on Tuesday said that its forces downed 297 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions overnight, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula. Russia’s overnight attack on Ukraine included anti-ship missiles, ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and more than 200 drones, Ukraine’s air force said. The strikes killed four people in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk regional military administration. The strikes across Ukrainian regions damaged homes, businesses and storage facilities, wounding at least five people, authorities said. Five people were wounded in the capital, Kyiv, according to officials. The Russian Defense Ministry said Tuesday that its forces struck metallurgical and chemical industries, the fuel and energy sector, and the military-industrial complex, as well as port infrastructure facilities in four regions of Ukraine. They included a Fire Point plant in Kyiv producing components for long-range cruise missiles and a tobacco factory in the central Poltava region used to make small arms ammunition, it said.
